source.title: When Should We Introduce Safety Interventions During Pretraining?
source.authors: Dylan Sam; Sachin Goyal; Pratyush Maini; A. Robey; J. Kolter

record.file_problem: not stated; the full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates harmful-request attack success under GCG suffix attacks, a different experimental setup relevant to whether suffixes bypass safety. It also evaluates safety after benign fine-tuning, but does not report a pre-fine-tuning comparison that establishes erosion.
record.gate_note: The paper measures attack success after GCG suffixes and after benign GSM8k fine-tuning. Figure 5's attack-success results are reported only graphically; the text describes differences by intervention timing and inference method. Figures 1 and 3 measure safety by intervention timing without the specified fine-tuning or attack, Figure 4 measures benign-request overrefusal, and Figure 6 measures probe separability; these do not test the listed versions. The paper does not measure per-token KL, compliant prefills, or safety localization in weights.
record.test_reason: The study compares when safety-pretraining data enters training (0/20/60/100%). It reports attack success after benign GSM8k fine-tuning (Fig 2) and under GCG suffixes (Fig 5) only to rank its own curriculum variants. The text never states how much benign fine-tuning or suffixes raise harmful compliance over the instruction-tuned models, and all values are figure-only. It therefore relies on the fine-tuning erosion and jailbreak findings as evaluation stress tests rather than testing them.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Under standard decoding, a delayed start (20–60%) gives the safest base and instruction-tuned models and the strongest post-benign-fine-tuning safety; Fig 2's caption says 0% or 20%, the text says ~20%. Under SafeBeam, a 0% start gives the best steerability. Earlier starts increase linear separability of safe vs unsafe content. On GCG, the 20%/60% robustness gain appears only under SafeBeam; Top-K jailbreakability does not noticeably change with timing, though the Discussion generalizes it.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies when pretraining safety interventions enter training, rather than testing the original fine-tuning or per-token KL methods. It includes a GCG suffix evaluation and benign fine-tuning evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: Intervention start timing (0%, 20%, 60%, 100%) and inference method (Top-K versus SafeBeam) change reported outcomes; the text says GCG robustness with SafeBeam improves at 20% or 60%, while standard-inference jailbreakability does not noticeably change with timing.

fits_no_version.finding: When safety-pretraining data enters training changes post-benign-fine-tuning and GCG ASR. Under Top-K, a ~20% start is safest after GSM8k fine-tuning; under SafeBeam, a 0% start is safest. Under SafeBeam, 20%/60% starts are more robust to GCG than 0%/100%; under Top-K, GCG ASR barely changes with timing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The timing of safety-pretraining interventions affects how robust safety is to later benign fine-tuning and suffix attacks.

record.problems: The relevant attack-success results are shown in figures without numerical values in the text. The paper does not give an un-attacked comparison for the GCG results, and the benign fine-tuning evaluation has no paired pre-fine-tuning result to establish erosion. The main experiments use 1.7B-parameter models in one pretraining setup.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version rows omitted. Figures 1 and 3 report safety outcomes by intervention timing without the specified fine-tuning or suffix attack; Figure 4 reports compliance on benign requests; Figures 6–8 report probe separability. These do not directly measure a listed claim version.

untested.parts: No explicit pre- versus post-benign-fine-tuning ASR comparison is stated in text or tables.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling or decoding attacks. GCG ASR has no stated no-attack comparison, and first-token bypass is not isolated.
Only a speculative hypothesis that early interventions may yield shallow heuristics; untested.
No training aimed at spreading safety beyond the first response tokens. Safety pretraining timing is a different intervention.

missing.what: Instruction-tuned ASR on standard safety benchmarks, a possible pre-fine-tuning and pre-attack reference. Its y-axis tops at 6%, versus 60% in Figs 2 and 5. The gap would bear on V2 and V4 only if the figures are readable, and the text never states the comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The study cites Qi et al. 2024a/b and treats benign-fine-tuning erosion and jailbreaks as background. All relevant numbers are figure-only; the reader's partial states for r12, r14 and r16 conflated timing comparisons with V4 effects. No verdict is given.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful fine-tuning experiment is reported.

Safety is evaluated after benign GSM8k fine-tuning, but no paired pre-fine-tuning result establishes whether fine-tuning raised harmful compliance. The after-fine-tuning results are retained as rows with cannot_determine state.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models is reported.
Tests GCG-learned suffixes, but not compliant prefilling or other adversarial suffix methods; does not isolate whether success comes from getting past the first response tokens.
No weight or rank localization experiment is reported.
The proposed explanation for safety being shallow is not tested.
No training specifically designed to spread safety beyond initial response tokens is reported.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: GCG suffix attacks, with intervention timing and inference method varied
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports that SafeBeam robustness to GCG jailbreaks depends on intervention timing, while standard-inference attack success does not noticeably change across timings; rows r9–r16. It does not report an un-attacked comparison or isolate a first-token bypass.
